2. [valid, your reading] find [an to-be-specified number of] issues that are, both [so I want two issues], possessing X and Y attributes.

> In Oct 2026, how many of us don't know this already?

The comments to this article suggest that it's still disputed.

Personally, I think it's a bit of a silly phrase, because it implies an absolute, and all anyone needs to do to disprove it is to show that coding was not solved for problem X. That's still the case -- it's just that the set of X is rapidly shrinking.

I think it's more indicative to say how much you trust LLM code. A little over a year ago, I scrutinised every line carefully, and it was buggy as hell and I had to fix most generated code by hand. Now, models write clean code with fewer bugs (far fewer) than I would. A year ago, I was doing a lot of steering during planning; now, it's rare that I don't agree with the model's first proposed solution, and even if I don't, it's most likely to fix a minor change in understanding, not to propose a substantial architectural change as it was before.

The one thing I'm not sure about is how much this is due to better prompting on my part. I doubt that this contributes much, but I still suspect that continual usage does make you more aware of what works and what does not: how much detail to provide, how to describe a problem or change, how to propose solutions while still leaving other options open.

children.author: prmph
children.text:
There are two main kinds of programmers:

Those who think the challenge is to overreach the limitations imposed by programming languages and types, etc, to do seemingly "magical" things. These are ones who would never understand why you might want higher-kinded types, the relative pros and cons of the functional vs imperative approaches, or even of type systems in general. They also tend to think the code written, in itself, is the valuable output of their work.

And then there are those who think the challenges is to model problem domain so well, using the language features, types and data structures, etc, that the solution (and further adjustments to it) becomes obvious and straightforward. They also tend to think the analysis and model that results is what is valuable.

Another way to see this difference: what impresses them? it is a hack that uses arcane knowledge to bypass software and hardware "limitation" or structures? Or is it code that is simple but still effective at solving complex problems in elegant ways, that may look simple but reflects a huge amount of knowledge, skill, and architectural intuition built up over many years?

I of course think that the second group are more effective and are doing proper programming, but many programmers and the general public think otherwise, or can't event tell the difference. I once worked with some colleagues could never see the light, despite a lot of support from me.

So here is the kicker, the dissonance in response to AI, I think, is kind of analogous to these two groups. The first groups likes that the AI will not stop them, but rather get them much quicker to their "magic", whereas the second group is more skeptical and sees many issues with AI not seeing the big picture and understanding deeper intent.
Learning syntax takes a weekend. Learning to approach problems analytically and algorithmically takes much longer, and is the only "hard part" of computer programming.
